incident_description:
I purchased the Marcy Club Revolution Trainer bike, model XJ-3220, made by Impex from Amazon on March 3, 2018 

On March 31, 2018 while operating the bike in a sitting flat road ride, my right foot slipped off the pedal and I was unable to recover in time to move my shin out of the way of the revolving bike pedal. The right pedal spun around at the accelerated rate of my ride and gouged my shin to the bone in one place, while deeply lacerating my shin in a second location.
 
I required twenty-seven stitches, two x-rays, and two hypodermic infusions of anesthesia directly into the tissue around the wound before the doctor could perform the repair procedure. 

Ten stitches sewed the remaining tissue under the skin close enough for the doctor to smooth the retracted upper skin over, attaching the upper skin with seventeen additional stitches to cover the wounds and avoid infection of the exposed bone. The other gaping areas required medical glue so the skin would not pull away and break the stitches before the bone deep wound could heal.

Not only did I miss a day of work that night, I was also on restrictive movement (including standing or walking) until the stitches were removed ten days later. The wound, healing from the outside in, caused me to often walk with a slight limp as the tissues slowly fused together. 

On close inspection of the bike pedal, after I removed the pieces of skin stuck on the right side between the metal rung and the canvas strap, I noticed the protruding plastic spikes attaching the reflectors. These reflector spikes are responsible for my shin gouge; and the pedalÃÂs uncovered jagged edges are responsible for the scraping lacerations on the sides of the gouge wounds, which have left life long scars.

This is a poorly manufactured and unsafe bike. For a few more dollars safety precautions could have been taken to cover the pedalÃÂs metal edges in soft rubberized plastic, and cut the pedal reflector spikes flush against the bike pedal's metal bracket. As a matter of fact, the pedal reflector has no real use on an indoor bike, and has caused injury, scarring, and a significant medical intervention.
justification: The incident resulted in severe injury requiring extensive medical treatment, including stitches and restricted movement, but no death was reported.

incident_description:
Based on my personal experience, I believe the newer full-face snorkel mask style is inherently dangerous, to experienced snorkelers as well as novices.  

I had snorkeled and polespear-fished for 30 years in coastal Mexican waters on annual sailing vacations, and have spent entire days snorkeling throughout the daylight hours, with never a problem in various conditions.  However, for a recent trip to Bali in October 2017, I splurged on a new full-face snorkel mask (I have dental tori that make the normal snorkel mouthpiece painful, over extended periods of wear.)   As a result, I came near death due to carbon monoxide rebreathing in a strong current.  I was unaware of the potential danger, going in.

My 20-something niece -- a daily surfer and strong swimmer who lives in Bali -- and I were swimming off the beach at Crystal Bay on Nusa Penida, heading to a small islet located about 600 feet away (Pulai Batumejinong).  I wore my snorkel mask and fins, while my niece was free swimming alongside me.  Due in part to language barriers, and the assumption our local companions would warn us of any issues, we (foolishly) did not inquire about local conditions ÃÂ I fully own that error.   Upon reaching the islet, a local boat came by to warn us of a strong current at that end of the islet, and my niece said she was scared, so upon the boatÃÂs departure, we decided to head immediately and directly back to the beach while we were still fresh, rather than explore the islet.

However, a very strong current was indeed coming off the beach, making it difficult to make headway.  I deliberately held my pace down to stay very close ahead of my niece because she did not have fins or snorkel, while I had my fins to propel me successfully against the current, so I was concerned for her.  (Upon later discussion, I learned that she, in turn, was holding back her own speed out of concern for me, as I was far less fit than she ÃÂ whereupon I pointed out to her that ÃÂat least fat floats.ÃÂ  ;)  )

The slow pace of our progress really concerned me, and I realized that I was growing tired enough that IÃÂd not be able to lend my niece any useful aid should she need it.  So, I gave the international distress wave to our friends on the beach, but they did not at first notice.  When at last they did notice, despite being major surfers they were unfamiliar with that signal and so did not realize I was asking for aid.  Seeing that they were not responding, I began swimming back in much harder, to overcome the current.  

Though I was indeed making slow progress against the current, I quickly found myself growing progressively weaker and out of breath ÃÂ something IÃÂd never experienced in my prior snorkeling experience, even when swimming hard to get back home after a long day meandering up a Mexican coastline.  I could not understand what was happening to me ÃÂ I vividly recall asking myself, again and again, ÃÂWhy is this so hard?! WhatÃÂs wrong with me?!ÃÂ  I would normally be able to maintain a strong kick for far longer, based on the pool training IÃÂd been doing prior to the trip.  I was not panicked, but did begin to grow first concerned and then scared that I wouldnÃÂt outlast my need to keep going.  I still did not panic, in part because I know drownproofing techniques, and can tread water with fins indefinitely; yet I did not want to be taken out to sea or up an unknown coastline.  I kept on plugging, swimming hard and breathing hard despite tiring and my growing weakness.  I made progress until at last (breathing extremely hard but regularly through the snorkel mask) I was able to set first a toehold, then a foothold onto the reef below me.  I rested a bit there, then continued in sufficiently further that our beach buddies (now alerted and aware) were able to walk/run out through the surf to drag me the rest of the way in, by now gasping for breath.  My niece followed, still swimming.

I was so weak I could barely stand, and the first thing my niece said was to ÃÂget that snorkel mask off her!ÃÂ  She and the others told me my lips were totally blue, and as I staggered up the sand and collapsed to sit on the beach, entirely spent and exhausted, she explained that she had read previously that there was a suspected problem with those snorkel masks.  

I must wholeheartedly concur.

While these masks may be considered by some to be acceptable in kiddie-pool conditions, I personally have come to believe they pose an inherent danger, since they will compromise the survivability of anyone who encounters unexpected conditions that require them to swim hard, using sustained strong effort.
justification: The incident involved a near-death experience due to carbon monoxide rebreathing from a full-face snorkel mask, indicating a high severity level. The occurrence likelihood is moderate as such incidents are not common but can happen under specific conditions.

incident_description:
Team One Powersports at 12899 Garrett Highway in Oakland, Maryland (Phone: 301-334-9494) sells the Oreion Motors Reeper offroad UTV product. Oreion Motors is located at  331 Academy Drive, Corrales, New Mexico 87048 (Phone: 505-916-1206). The Oreion Reeper's engine is mounted in the middle of the vehicle, directly behind and between the driver and passenger. The engine and transmission stick forward through a large opening in the steel engine firewall between the vehicle occupants and the engine with no fire-proof safety cover over the engine firewall opening. All that separates the vehicle occupants from the engine is a flimsy piece of plastic with a very low melting temperature. If there was ever an engine fire in the vehicle the center console cover would melt almost instantly, a rubber gasoline hose attached to the front of the engine would also likely melt very quickly and the vehicle occupants would suffer severe burns as a melted fuel hose would squirt fuel directly into the driver / passenger compartment. This vehicle should include a steel cover over the engine firewall opening to protect the driver / passengers in the event of a fire. This is a very severe design and manufacturing defect and an easily remedied safety defect. Oreion Motors could easily cover the engine firewall opening with a steel cover but it seems they use plastic to save money. This vehicle is a safety risk to everybody who owns one and everybody who rides in one. The first person who suffers an engine fire in this vehicle design may die or be severely injured by burns as a result of this design and manufacturing defect. The easy, simple remedy to this dangerous safety risk is to add a metal engine firewall cover over the engine firewall opening to protet the driver and occupants of the vehicle in case of an engine fire. This picture shows the opening directly next to where the seats would be installed and illustrates the design defect and safety hazard well:
http://img901.imageshack.us/img901/1157/KAohPF.jpg
justification: The description highlights a severe design defect that could lead to severe burns or death in the event of an engine fire, but no actual incident has occurred yet.

You see Can Am refuses to acknowledge there is a problem, refuses to issue a recall or offer to fix the problem, but yet they will sell you a repair harness for $50 to fix it yourself. Understand, there is such heat build up within these 3 wires that it causes the insulating wire casing to completely melt off all 3 wires. And the fact that they are within an inch of the gas tank vent and rubber fuel lines should concern EVERYONE involved. This whole problem stems from the wires being undersized in the design of the electrical system.
 
Another issue I recently experienced with this exact same atv in which Can Am actually did issue a recall on but claims my atv did not fall under was the "Risk of loss control hazard". During a ride a year or better ago we were traveling down a trail with a gradual turn to the right. Without warning the atv steering locked or jammed not allowing the rider to steer left or right causing the atv to leave the trail and go down over a 100' embankment. Fortunately the rider was not severely hurt and able to jump off before the atv left the trail. I find it very ironic that my atv experienced the exact symptoms Can Am issued a recall for but was not included in the recall. I feel this problem is a lot more widespread than they like to acknowledge. For what its worth my atv experienced a significant about of damage due to that steering failure.
justification: The incident involved a steering failure leading to an accident, but the rider was not severely hurt, indicating an injury did not occur.

A few minutes later; the operator, standing next to the snowmobile, pushed the SHOT Starter button to start the engine.  We believe the throttle had not been exercised since it was shut off and remained in the closed position (idle position).  The snowmobile immediately accelerated to full throttle, traveled approximately 95ÃÂ, hit our [REDACTED], became airborne and slammed into our barn.  The engine remained at full throttle in contact with the barn until the tether cord was pulled.  The throttle lever was still in the closed position when the tether cord killed the engine.  We are thankful no one was hurt, we believe the snowmobile is totaled.  The snowmobile has about 350 miles on it.

The dealer downloaded data from the on-board control module that confirmed the throttle position sensor maintained a 41 degree open "stuck" reading in the last 38 seconds of operations.

Case Number [REDACTED]
Consumer Product Safety Officer, Regulatory Operations and Regions Branch
Health Canada / Government of Canada
[REDACTED] / Tel: 416-973-4312 / Fax: 416-973-1746

Since this time I have been contacted by a representative of the Canadian Tire Corporation, the company from which I purchased the Inversion chair and they had told me I would be hearing from Impex fitness the company that distributes this line of fitness Equipment.
[REDACTED] from Impex fitness e-mailed Jan 3 2018 asking me when it would be a good time to talk about my accident. I responded to the email and we eventually talked.

When performing normally, an AT ski-boot allows you to unlock or lock the flex to suit your purpose, whether skiing downhill or walking uphill. In the case of skiing downhill, a skier wants their boot to be locked, providing complete support through aggressive turns. 

The Scarpa Maestrale RS has a weak pin that is prone to rupturing mid run and dramatically affecting a skier's performance. In my case, this has occurred five times between both boots, and it's after the most recent occurrence that I've decided to contact you today. When the pin breaks, a skier's ankle support collapses and can often lead to a dramatic crash at speed. In my most recent case, the pin ruptured in the midst of a long, steep pitch of skiing in the backcountry. I somersaulted over sideways and was fortunate to self-arrest and prevent further falls. 

Scarpa offers pins for repair in high quantity, suggesting that this is in fact a known defect from their team, and rather than fix the product, they seek to put a band-aid on the fault until the next break. Their updated Maestrale RS boots have completely redesigned the ski/walk mode, again suggesting a known defect.
justification: The incident describes a product defect leading to dramatic crashes, with one instance resulting in a somersault and self-arrest, indicating potential for injury.

incident_description:
I experienced an emergency while snorkeling with a full-face Tribord mask a couple of years ago. I had snorkeled with the mask each day for several days before so it took me by surprise. I was having a great time with the mask because it never fogged, I could see so clearly all around and it was a beautiful day. This day I was on Kahekili beach on Maui floating just over the reef. I had been out for longer than normal because the conditions were so good and with that mask, it's easier to stay out longer because there are fewer issues with the mask or snorkel than with the 2-piece systems.

I realized I should head back to shore so I signaled my husband and we were gradually headed back that way when all of a sudden I realized that I had been relaxed and had forgotten to breathe. So reflexively, I took a deep gasp which then suctioned the mask to my face I tried to signal my husband I was in trouble, began puling on the mask but I couldn't get it off due to the suction and without having my feet down yet, it was hard to get a good stance to really pull with my arms. I did get it off. I believe I pushed out whatever air I had left and peeled it off thankfully just as I started to black out. Just barely in time without a moment to spare.

I have never been more scared. It was very similar to sleep apnea experiences I have had when I woke up gasping, only this time, it was like I was gasping with a plastic bag stuck to my face. I have obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) so when I am really relaxed my narrow airway can close. I was really relaxed in the mask and I am wondering if my airway closed and the nature of the full face mask prevented me from re-opening my airway. I am grateful I was able to get the mask off and get back to the beach.

I absolutely love the mask, but I am beginning to suspect that with OSA I need to be mindful of clear breathing techniques and regular breaks if I am to use it. I think that is the benefit of a traditional snorkel. You can never forget what you are doing, you are breathing through your mouth deliberately, and it encourages you to focus more on your breathing technique. The traditional mask fogs, leaks water, forces you to take breaks and that is probably a very good thing.

It happened August 23, 2016 when I was 44 years old and in good health. I am an OK swimmer and comfortable in the water.
justification: The incident involved a near-drowning experience due to a full-face snorkeling mask suctioning to the face, but no actual injury or death occurred.

During a target shooting and sighting-in session in my backyard... After cranking  the crossbow, then loading an arrow, I placed the crossbow on top of my shooting table and prepared to shoot at my target. While pointing at the target (fortunately), With my left hand, I moved the Safety to FIRE position.  The crossbow fired instantly.  My trigger finger was NOT on the trigger. My right had was completely on the stock grip.  I was in such shock, I could not believe what just happened. 

I immediately called the manufacturer Ravin, and informed them and requested they replace the trigger mechanism because I had no faith in it.  I returned the crossbow to them, and they actually sent me a new crossbow.  I did have a previous issue before this incident whereby the bow did NOT fire with the Safety on Fire position.

The manufacturer informed me that this type of incident can happen when the arrow is not completely pushed-in until you hear a loud click sound.  Apparently, when the arrow nock is not completely inserted into the trigger assembly, it causes the trigger mechanism to not engage fully.  
This is why they are recalling the White nocks installed on their arrows and replacing them with a slightly shorter and tighter-on-the-string nock. This was my first Ravin R9 Crossbow.

After receiving my replacement crossbow Serial #: 50114, I spent several days sighting it in and shooting it at my targets. No incidents, bow working as expected.
One day while target shooting, a friend stopped by to say hi, and since I did not want to shoot while he was next to me (I like to have full concentration), I decided to UNCOCK the bow.  Now, this is something no other crossbow can do.  Normally with other crossbows, once they are loaded or crancked up, one must fire an arrow into a target or ground with a special ÃÂdischargeÃÂ arrow in order to unload or discharge the crossbow.

So I proceeded to uncock the bow, and as I was doing that, the handle slipped out of my right hand and unwound so fast and violently that it hit the tips of 3 of my finger, cracking one (my finger tips were black n blue for over one week) and scared the ÃÂdaylightsÃÂ out of me and caused lots of pain.  In addition to hitting my fingers, the handle hit the scope and broke the right turret knob, and made 2 gashes on the stock.

The reason this happened is because the crancking handle had a very small straight handle grip that basically you hold with 2 fingers, and this is NOT secure enough to hold back the weight force uncocking the bow.

Again, I contacted Ravin - the manufacturer, and again they agreed to replace the crossbow. I suggested to them that they improve the grip on the handle.

To my pleasant surprise, the crancking handle grip on the replacement crossbow (Serial #: 50114), was now round and offered a much firmer grip than the original design.  I suspect Ravin has has this same issue (handle slipping out of hand) quite a few times, which lead them to change the design.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (cracked finger and bruises) due to the handle slipping during uncocking, indicating a severity level of 3. The occurrence likelihood is 3 (possible) as the issue was addressed by the manufacturer, suggesting it was not an isolated event.

incident_description:
I was hunting with the Ravin R9 crossbow for 3 weeks in November and frequently noticed the nock was not fully engaging with the string. This was my first year to crossbow hunt, as I used a compound bow for 25 years, so I kept thinking I was doing something wrong. I told my husband it kept happening, but he also thought it was user error. One evening after hunting I was going to discharge my arrow into a target to unload it and the bow did not go off.  I put the bow on safety and when  I attempted to re-nock the arrow the bow went off and the string snapped my left hand. My middle finger, pointer and thumb were struck and immediately turned swollen and blue. I developed a black string blister on all 3 fingers. I was unable to use my hand for at about 10 days. I still have a scar and calloused mark especially on my middle finger that hasn't healed completely. 

I am reporting this incident now because up until I heard about this recall, I thought I did something in error that caused my injuries.  Now I know this was due to faulty nocks.
justification: The incident resulted in injury with swollen and blue fingers, a black string blister, and lasting scars, indicating a severity level of 3. The occurrence likelihood is 3 (possible) as the issue was noticed frequently but not every time.

incident_description:
The consumer indicates that he has had to take his UTV to the dealership three to four times for repairs to its transmission and to its back-end. The transmission is not engaging correctly as when switching from low or high to reverse it will grind. The only way to get the transmission to switch is to shove it into gear however it will still grind. At this point, the consumer needs to put the transmission into parking and then try to put it in reverse. The consumer has only noted the grinding problem when the UTV is in four-wheel drive, and he has ran ten to twenty miles on it.

The grinding of the transmission is attempted to be mimicked multiple times at the dealership however they have been unsuccessful as they are unable to ride it ten to twenty miles in the lot. The one time that they ran it this long, the representative informed the consumer that the UTV was not in four-wheel rive mode.

05/2016: The UTV was remedied under a recall for posing a fire hazard. Unit caught fire after the recall and it was fixed.

At one point in early 2016, the consumer was informed by representatives that the dealership used transmission parts from a RZR 1000 to see if it would fix the issues his RZR 900 was having however it did not work; the consumer is unaware if the dealership switched back to transmission parts for a RZR 900 on his unit.

The consumer states that the unit is used once or twice during warmer seasons, and has two to three-thousand miles on it to date. The consumer plans on keeping his UTV for at least the next thirty days in case an investigation ensues however, at the moment, the UTV sits at the dealership for the continued transmission grinding problem.
justification: The incident involves mechanical issues with the UTV's transmission but no reported injuries or deaths.

incident_description: I purchased a Ninebot by Segway miniPRO from a company called More4Mini.  I ordered it with off road tires and a handlebar.  When it arrived, we put the handle bar on it and road it a little then took it to the shop to charge it.  That evening I rode it all over in the shop with no issues.  The next morning, I completed the tutorial on my phone application and took off on our dead end street to ride it from one house to the next.  I got about 150 feet down the road and one of the tires locked up.  The Segway twisted and threw me down the asphalt.  I had bruises on my knee, butt, and arm, as well as road rash up my arm.  I also hit my head on the asphalt.  I ended up losing conscientiousness and had to go to the emergency room.  Thankfully I didn't have a concussion, nor any broken bones.  My knee was swollen for a couple weeks and the doctor said I tore something in my shoulder.  I did get in contact with the More4Mini place and was told the Segway wheel should not have locked up on me.  I am waiting to get all my medical bills in to present them to the company to see if they will pay them or not.

I purchased my API stand from Bass Pro about 4 years ago.  On Sunday it suffered a total structural failure while I was using it.  The standing platform cracked in half, suddenly with out warning..  Luckily, I was in a full harness and my fall was arrested.  

 As background information, I have used this stand about 30 times.  I also have kept it inside when stored and never left it out in the elements for more than a day or 2.  I've always used care in using the stand as not to put undue wear on it.  When the stand failed, I was climbing up the tree.  At the time of failure, I was standing on the platform and not moving either the top or bottom section of the stand.  The failure was sudden and fast, it was like the floor dropped out. 

The pictures attached show the failure points.  It failed at the location where the foot strap is connected to the standing platform.  In this location, there is less structural material.  It is also where your feet attached to the stand when climbing, and the pressure of downward force is focused.
justification: The incident involved a sudden structural failure of the stand, but the user was unharmed due to wearing a full harness, which arrested the fall.

Company. They refunded my money. I bought another. It worked as long as the previoua device and the. Burned my arm again.  The user blog has over 165 entries from consumers who have been burned. Fitbit has not recalled the model.


On the Fitbit site, search burn and Charge hr. ItÃÂs all there. With pictures of injured consumers.

incident_description: I purchased an Apple Watch, 1st generation, the day they became available. In July 2017, I noticed two, small, full thickness skin lesions on my left wrist adjacent to the watch. As severe as the lesions appeared, I had no recollection of pain of receiving them. I joked I had a flesh-eating bacteria. I took the watch off for several weeks until the lesions healed over. I again started to wear the watch. Within 2 days, I developed another more severe full thickness skin burn adjacent to the Apple Watch. I contacted the company and was told it was an allergy to the strap. I had already, independently for another reason, been allergy tested for nickel and methacrylate and was found not allergic. There ingredients are in the watch. I bought a $150 leather strap, waited weeks for this, now, third apparent burn, to heal over. I put the watch back on with the leather strap and within two days I had two more full thickness burns on my left wrist adjacent to the watch. I have spent hours upon hours on the phone and in emails with Apple Safety. They refuse to take the watch back to even examine it. They deny that the watch played any role in what happened. I reported the issue to the Better Business Bureau but Apple's response was that the device was out of warranty and closed the case. If something is out of warranty, it is allowed to stop working but it cannot harm the consumer. The watch seems to be causing small electrocution-type injuries to my wrist. I now have stopped wearing it, but how do I know a new Apple Watch may not do the same since Apple has not looked into this? Or perhaps they have and just are not admitting it.....
justification: The incident caused full thickness skin burns, which is an injury, so the severity level is 3.

incident_description:
Purchased a Barnett Raptor FX3 crossbow which came with two 20in Headhunter carbon bolts (arrows).

Upon attempting to shoot one of the bolts for the very first time, it came apart in the process of leaving or shortly after leaving the bow.  The front landed  about 30 yrds  away and the rear landed about 15yrds away.

The shear was fairly clean near the center of the label, approx 9 inches from the rear of the bolt.

Date on the bolt was 2016 10 10 

I used 3 other bolts on the bow without incident, so I know it was not the bow.  

I have seen others on the internet report similar things with another "brand" but I wonder if both brands were manufactured in the same factory at the same time.

I suspect that the process of putting on the labels at the factory damaged the bolts creating a weak spot.

Obviously a risk of injury to the shooter and bystanders, or risk of property damage from the separated pieces of the bolt.  Furthermore, improper resistance from the bolt could cause damage to the crossbow and/or structural failure, which may then cause injury to the shooter or other bystanders/observers.
justification: The incident involved a bolt breaking during use, posing a risk of injury or property damage, but no actual injury was reported.

incident_description:
I was riding a product brand-named "ElliptiGo" which is an exercise machine that rides outdoors like a bicycle, but the rider stands on two pedals and makes a motion similar to an elliptical trainer to propel the machine.  The rider holds bicycle-like handlebars that are attached to a long vertical metal pole, which in turn is attached to the platform on which the rider stands.  I was badly injured when that metal pole separated from the base platform resulting in the handlebars being essentially unattached to the machine.

I was traveling on a straight and level, paved, clean, wide bicycle path on a dry temperate day, so there were no such contributing factors to my fall.  I was traveling on the Elliptigo one moment, and the next thing I knew I was crumpled up around the Elliptigo on the ground with a broken wrist, bad concussion and a severe laceration from a blow to my face.  The handlebar pole I've described was separated from the rest of the machine and the handlebars were turned around from the impact.

I had always had my machine professionally serviced by a local bike shop that is also an ElliptiGo dealer.  My machine had actually been the subject of an earlier recall.  I had brought my machine to this bicycle shop to make the repair necessary to comply with the recall, and the repair was made at that time.  I have always had them perform service on my machine.  I was also very aware of the operating requirements for the machine, and had checked the machine before riding to make sure everything was properly adjusted and secured, including the latch which secures the handle bar pole.
justification: The incident resulted in a broken wrist, concussion, and severe laceration, indicating a severity level of 3 (Injury). The occurrence likelihood is rated 2 (unlikely) as the machine had been professionally serviced and checked before use, suggesting such failures are not common.

While hanging on the wall (fortunately not while riding), the front tire blew off the rim and the inner tube was shredded.  The tires itself is damaged beyond repair.  No one was injured in this incident, but if someone had been riding the bike at the time or had been in the vicinity, they could have been injured.

The tire brand is Vee Tire Company.  Model is Apache Fatty Slick.

incident_description: I was riding my 2013 Trek 8.3 DS bicycle (S/N: WTU199C7229G) today and stopped at the traffic light to cross Aviation Boulevard. When I resumed riding the front wheel seized up after 30 feet. After hauling the bike out of the road and examining it I noticed that the pot metal casting of the front fork where it holds the wheel axle in place had broken off causing the axle to shift and the quick release lever to jam in the front brake disk seizing up the wheel. Fortunately I was accelerating from a stop and going slow when the failure occurred or I would have been thrown over the handlebars and possibly injured. The bike dealer I purchased the bike from said that they were going to register it with Trek when I purchased it in March 2013 but I never received a recall notice.

incident_description: In July 2017 I purchased a Look 795 Light bicycle, which is distributed in the USA by Hawley, LLC.  While riding my new bicycle, the chain did not catch the chain ring and fell off when I tried to shift gears causing me to nearly fall off the bicycle.  I was forced to pull to the side of the road and walk my bike over 2 miles for relief. I am aware of a least 1 other rider who has had experienced the same malfunction with the bike described above.

incident_description: We recently had a bicycle rim problem in which the tire blew sideways off the rim. This was a relatively new bicycle wheel, complete with hub, spokes and rim for the front wheel of our bicycle. We bought it from Hostel Shoppe in July 2016, for $215. Our previous rim was about 14 years old from a different mfg; it had 16,000 miles on it. We had retired that rim as it had a small crack in the aluminum. This is on a RANS SCREAMER bicycle, a recumbent tandem. We are a retired couple, age 68, and have been riding road bikes for 45 years, well over 100,000 miles. We are responsible adults and ride safely, never had an accident. We have ridden our recumbent tandem about 17,000 miles, always with the same brand tire; a Comet Primo Kevlar,  100psi tire. This is the best tire one can buy, $53 each. the tire that blew off was only about 40% worn. The rim was model 20" Cliffhanger, manufactured by Velocity. The tire blow off happened after a ride when we were stopped, talking to a neighbor. If it had happened while riding we would have wrecked and probably had serious injuries. There is no doubt as to the reason for the blowoff. The Cliffhanger rims have a very short flange on which the tire bead seats / contacts. About half the flange height / rim contact of rims we had previously ridden for 100,000+ miles. We were concerned about this rim flange from the time of purchase in July 2016, but went ahead and used it because that it is the rim that Hostel Shoppe sells on their new recumbent tandems. We reported this failuire to Hostel Shoppe and Velocity wheel company. The Velocity rep said last winter they changed the rim flange design, to meet some industry rim standard. They did not recall old rims, nor did they intend to. They replaced our rim, free and Hostel Shoppe laced the new, different model rim on our hub. Hostel Shoppe also replaced our $53 tire. We were thankful to get a new wheel and tire at no cost, but disappointed that this Cliffhanger rim is still being sold. It should be taken off the market. Recumbent tandems often go at speeds over 30 mph and the forward rider is essentially sitting right above the wheel. A blowoff while riding would cause serious wreck and injuries, possibly even death. As said above we are lifetime bike riders, with many miles. We have never had a equipment failure, except for chains. There is no doubt in our minds that the Cliffhanger rim is a defective design and that more tire blowoffs will occur due to the short flange height. Hope you will get this rim off the market. Thanks [REDACTED]
justification: The incident involved a tire blowoff that could have caused serious injuries if it happened while riding, but no actual injuries occurred.

incident_description:

Again, with such minimal use, I believe this problem represents either a design/engineering problem, or the use of substandard parts and materials. incident_description: On August 12, 2017 at approximately 12:30 pm, I went to my storage building to pick up my 2014 Polaris Ranger 570 Crew, which I was going to use to haul my boat cover and other items from the beach at my lake cabin in [REDACTED]. I started and briefly warmed up the Ranger, and backed it out of the storage building.  I then drove my car into the storage building and closed the overhead door.  The Ranger was idling for a total of about 2 minutes. The only thing in the rear box or bed of the Ranger was a boat cover that was inside of a plastic tote, and some hand tools. There were no explosives or gas cans in the Ranger or its box/bed. I then drove the Ranger about 2 1/2 miles from my storage building to my lake cabin.  I parked the Ranger in my driveway and shut off the ignition.  About 10 minutes later, I heard 2 explosions. About this same time, my wife and next door neighbor yelled for me to come and help them.  When I ran to my driveway, I observed that the Ranger was fully engulfed in flames. Debris from the Ranger was all over the yard, including a tailgate latch that was thrown 75 feet from the Ranger. The flames destroyed surrounding property, including a large tree, landscaping, and the concrete driveway underneath. My wife's car sustained thermal damage. No persons were injured. Two rural fire departments and the [REDACTED] responded. I have extensive photos and videos of the incident, but this Website appears not to be Mac compatible for uploading. The Ranger's fuel tank was approximately 3/4 full.  I filled the tank approximately 2 weeks prior. I noticed nothing unusual about the Ranger prior to parking it in my driveway.  There were no gas odors, and the engine ran normally. I did not notice any warning lights on the dash.
justification: The incident involved a vehicle fire causing property damage but no injuries, making it a severity level 2. Such events are rare, hence an occurrence likelihood of 1.

I slowly brought the engine RPM's up but the firing was inconsistent (missing/popping). I noticed that smoke was coming from the exterior part of the muffler (not the exhaust port) and it had increased the temperature of the surrounding plastic to well over 200 degrees. incident_description: I purchased a 2016 Polaris Outlaw 110 EFI youth ATV for my 12 year old Granddaughter from Road, Track & Trail in [REDACTED] on 6ÃÂ·27-17. The seller had inspected and serviced the ATV and it appeared to be In very good condition. But since the purchase I have had several what I think are serious safety issues with it due to bad design. We ride at the Rocky Glen OHV Park in [REDACTED]. This park is 120 acres of varied terrain with plenty of dirt, mud and wet conditions. My Granddaughter is an experienced rider and this is her third season of riding. Problems associated with the Polaris Outlaw 110 EFI youth ATV1. The vent tube for the gas tank comes off the side of the gas tank filler neck allowing gasoline to leak out. This is particularly dangerous When transporting the ATV in an enclosed vehicle or trailer due to the accumulation of gasoline fumes.2. Most of the wiring connections are not protection from water or moisture damage. In my case this caused an electrical failure making the engine stop running while my Granddaughter was riding it. Luckily she was not hurt. I found the problem to be a bullet type connector where the male connector was brass and the female connector was plated, the moisture cause a reaction of dissimilar metals and the connection failed causing the engine to stop running.3. The CVT transmission housing has two open ended vent pipes that can allow dirt and moisture to enter the housing and cause it to malfunction. Mine has not malfunctioned yet but the possibility is there. In the owners manual they even show where there is a drain plug on the housing to drain water if it enters, so they know this is a problem. The drum brakes are not sealed in any way and do not work very well when wet which is a serious safety hazard. The thumb throttle is a poor design for younger riders. In my Granddaughters case her thumb gets fatigued in a short time making it difficult to operate the throttle. She has to stop riding and rest her thumb. This is a safety hazard when she is riding. Please note. My complaint is against Polaris not the seller Road, Track & Trail.

incident_description:
I recently experienced a major issue with my Sherwood AVID BCD (Buoyancy Control Device). This is the device all diver wear that holds the inflation bladder and attaches the scuba tank to their bodies. I have been a NAUI, SDI/TDI Dive Instructor since 2003. I have used many different brands of gear over the years and have never had a BCD do this. This AVID BCD is approx. 6 years old but only has 4-5 dives on it. It has sat, unused, in my air-conditioned house. While I realize this does have some years on it, it has only been used 4-5 times! Upon doing a giant stride entry into the pool, demonstrating the skill for a student, I felt my tank free-floating off to the side once I was in the water. The weird part is it was pulling my 2nd stage regulator out of my mouth (this is the part of the scuba gear that comes from your tank and supplies your air via a regulator in your mouth). On a typical BCD, the tank is attached to the BCD via "Cam buckles", or a locking mechanism designed to grip the tank and secure it to the vest. I've had tanks slip out in the past, but this is an obvious design flaw and I believe Sherwood should do an instant recall on these before someone gets seriously hurt or even killed out in open water when this happens to them. If this were to happen in open water, in the ocean with waves and current, the manner in which the cam buckles break/fail will cause the tank to simply float away from the diver. Imagine being 50 feet underwater and your tank simply break free from your vest, pulling the regulator (your only air supply) out of your mouth. This would result in the diver either doing an emergency accent (possibly causing an air embolism) or finding a diver to share air with for a controlled accent. Either outcome could be disastrous. I have read numerous others having this EXACT same issue with the AVID BCD on numerous different scuba forums, so I know the manufacturer, Sherwood Scuba, is aware of the problem. To date, I have not been able to locate a recall or offer to repair this BCD. I have contacted Sherwood Scuba, via email, with no response.

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident describes a serious equipment failure that could lead to injury or death, but no actual injury occurred in this case.

incident_description:
The incidents concern an Aeris A300 CS scuba diving computer.  This computer has now failed in 3 separate incidents (in a potentially life-threatening manner) since I purchased it June 28, 2016.  The first time (Sept. 2016), on changing the battery, all information concerning previous dives was erased, contrary to the statements in the manual that this information is remembered.  This means the computer no longer has nitrogen saturation information which is used to determine allowable dive parameters such as how long one can safely stay at particular depths.  The only remedy is to not dive for 24 hours, but even this may not fully account for this issue.   I returned the unit for warranty service.  At this time, Aeris had been merged with Oceanic (both companies were owned by American Underwater Products) and the merger announcement stated that all Aeris warranties were now honored by Oceanic and, indeed, they repaired the unit under warranty.  

The second and third incidents occurred about a year later (August 2017).  Again, a battery issue caused the computer to lock up in the middle of a dive while I was at a depth of approximately 60 feet. The unit is supposed to give a "low battery" warning but in this case it simply died with no warning in the middle of a dive.  Again, this is potentially life threatening since one relies on the logged information to safely ascend without risking decompression sickness (DCS).  I determined that the problem was the battery had died, but with no warning.  The third incident occurred a few days later and this time, the computer screen suddenly cracked in the middle of a dive (again at about 60 ft), carrying the same life threatening implications.  The danger of both of these failures is compounded because the computer also indicates how much air is remaining in the tank.

I returned the unit to the manufacturer but now, Oceanic has been purchased by another company (Huish) and they claim that they no longer warrant Aeris products.  They  claim that Huish bought Oceanic, but without any involvement with Aeris, despite the previous statement that Oceanic would honor Aeris warranties.  

The actual computer is manufactured by a company called Pelagic Pressure Systems and Oceanic appears to market the same computer under their brand name  (model VTX).  I spoke with representatives of both Oceanic and Pelagic and neither company would honor the warranty or even offer a paid repair option.  Further, when I described the 3 incidents above, neither company responded to the potential safety issues I have mentioned, nor did they show any interest in examining the unit in light of these failures.  Recall that Oceanic did service the unit under warranty for the first incident just a year ago.

I feel there are two issues:

1. There is a possible safety issue with this dive computer which, under the right circumstances could be life-threatening.
2.  Refusing to honor the warranty seems unfair and irresponsible under these circumstances. It seems particularly irresponsible not to examine the unit for information concerning the failures. Many units are in service.

incident_description:
My grandson and his cousin were playing on this Flexible Flyer Play Park Swing Set, Model 46604T, when one of the four bar attachments to the lawn swing came apart and they crashed to the ground.  My wife and I bought this for them around October 2016 for their Christmas present.  The problem is that the phillips screw goes into a threaded sleeve that has a hex head on it with a lock washer.  There are two pieces of black plastic that straddle each of the four bars and this screw and sleeve hold it all together. If you tighten this up too much, then the swing will not swing smoothly because the black plastic is being squeezed too much and making a terrible noise. They should have used a longer screw that would have bottomed out or tightened in the sleeve. 
We bought the same model for my son's kids and he just had the same thing happen with his 5 yr old on the two seater air glider.  Only difference was that his son hit the ground hard and ended up in the ER this week. Xrays showed that he had no injuries and was released to go home. My son will be contacting also.

incident_description: Commercial slide produced by SR Smith ("Vortex").  A child was climbing up the slide ladder and fell off the ladder onto the deck below it.  There is no defect in the slide, or ladder; however, the question is whether the idea of a metal ladder at 8 - 9 feet of height is appropriate for the slide.  The slide is sold with two options:  a ladder and a stair kit.  Our slide was purchased with the ladder.  The ladder provides access at a steeper angle and requires more coordination and strength to climb. A ladder provides no protection for a fall backwards. The concern is whether a ladder access to the slide top is appropriate given the other concepts around a summer pool.  For example, the ladder is always wet, and while the stair treads have a rough surface, the hand railings can get slippery when they are wet.  Also, children wear sun screen, which is very slipper, and makes the railing slick.  A stairway, while presenting some of the same problems, appears to be a much better solution and we will likely be changing our ladder to a stairway as a result of the fall.  The child that fell will thankfully suffer no long term injuries, but the fall from the top of the ladder indicated to me that there is a potential safety hazard that should be addressed - possibly by discontinuing the option of an open ladder to such a commercially offered slide and instead only selling it with a stairway.  The fall also appears to have nothing to do with the treads, it wasn't a missed step or slip, the child fell straight backwards onto the deck below, it seems it was more a result of missing the coordination necessary to hold the steep railing while climbing up- something that a stair kit would assist.
justification: The child fell from a significant height but suffered no long-term injuries, indicating a severity level of 2. The likelihood of recurrence is high (4) due to the ladder's design and environmental factors like wetness and sunscreen.

incident_description:
I have a 4 year old Hayward model H400FDN natural gas swimming pool heater, for an in-ground pool. I recently found the clear and painted power and temperature control plastic "lens" for the control panel, on the ground, having become unglued. The control panel has slots in it where rain can easily enter the circuit board, mounted directly beneath it, and connected to the electronic control buttons, causing the electronics to be exposed to water and creating a potential electrical shock hazard, as well as causing a short and failure of the circuit board. This is an incredibly poor design, and more importantly, a dangerous design, especially centered around a swimming pool, where barefoot bathers will come in contact with the electronic controls. In addition, a replacement for this is over $150. This could have easily been avoided had the design for the lens been large enough to be held in place by the surrounding bezel, which curiously has a foam gasket around it in an attempt to keep moisture out. I've emailed the company and the response was to merely purchase a replacement part at over $150 and they gave me retail pool dealers where I can purchase this part. Because of this poor design, and because of the potential of a shock hazard, I am contacting this office of The Consumer Product Safety Commission to look into the lack of safety inherent in this design.
The CPSC response, Release # [REDACTED], informed me of a different model gas heater, model [REDACTED], and Hayward's voluntary recall of a circuit board failure, and the resultant buildup of dangerous amounts of gas and the possibility of explosion and/or fire. This is of similar concern to rain water entry onto the circuit board on my model, H400FDN, and adds to my concerns about a bather's potential for electric shock, the possibility of gas buildup and explosion. "Hazard: A malfunctioning circuit board can cause these gas pool heaters to fail to ignite, allowing gas to accumulate in the heater cover. Delayed ignition of built-up gas can result in a fire or explosion causing property damage and injuries."   

Thank you,
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident describes a potential for electric shock, gas buildup, and explosion, which could lead to death. The likelihood is possible due to the poor design and exposure to water.

Upon registering the bike online and initiating an inquiry regarding the issue over the weekend after returning home, Pacific Cycle initially tried to convince me that the damage must be the product of my being sold a refurbished bike by Walmart.com because of its 2012 manufacture date, before finally admitting that used bikes can only be purchased directly from Pacific Cycle and settling on incorrect installation of the pedal as cause for the damage. As I had explained to Pacific Cycle on more than one occasion, however, this could not have been the case, as I had never previously encountered any problems with the pedal over the course of a full year of heavy and regular usage (primarily to and from the local grocery stores -- the nearest of which is a over a mile away -- on at least a monthly basis, but also to my P.O. Box at the Pio Nono Post Office more than 4 miles away). Moreover, I have been very careful to avoid exposing the bike to the elements, keeping it indoors when not in use and not riding it in the rain or through water/puddles. In the absence of prior ownership, any indication that the pedal was installed incorrectly or exposure of the crank assembly to moisture, the damage to the crank assembly threading can only have been caused by the use of inadequate or substandard materials in the construction of it, which should warrant a recall all Pacific Cycle crank assemblies composed of the same materials.
justification: The incident involved a pedal falling off without causing injury, indicating a severity level of 2. The occurrence likelihood is 3 (possible) as the issue appears to stem from material quality rather than common misuse.

incident_description:
I am a bicycle mechanic in Portland, OR. I was doing a repair on a Kinn bicycle (their Cascade Flyer model) and noticed a major and potentially fatal design flaw. 
There is a electrical contact point (I believe it would be called a carbon brush) on the inside of the head tube which hits the steerer tube on the fork right above the fork crown (meant as a ground for a taillight). On the bike I was working the contact has worn a 1/8" deep grove into the steerer tube on the fork. This part of the bike is the point with the highest amount of stress. Any damage there could case the steerer tube to separate from the fork. This would obviously cause a crash, which would be very dangerous to the rider. Also this bike was specifically designed to carry children on the back of it. Which makes this even more concerning.
I definitely would recommend that anyone who has one of these bike discontinue riding them immediately and take it to a professional bicycle mechanic to have it looked at. The situation could be remedied by replacing the fork, if damaged, and removing the carbon brush from the inside of the head tube.
justification: The design flaw could cause a crash, posing a high risk of injury or death, especially since the bike is designed to carry children.

A weld in weight bench came undone.  It appears it is a defect in manufacturing and because of where the weld is and used by consumers like myself to hold several hundred pounds above our heads.. a serious concern.

The item is a Dicks Fitness Gear Olympic Weight Bench.
Model #: PROOB-600
Style #: STE00103

The item was purchased in 2014-2015 and only used lightly for a few months before storing it away.  My oldest son brought it out from storage and was setting it up and noticed that a critical weld on one of the base had come clean off the mounting plate.  

I had emailed Dick's Sporting Good about the issue, including pictures, and they stated that because the item is over a year old that I need to contact the manufacturer.  The Dick's representative then spent a good amount of time tracking down who the manufacturer was as it was under a different name.  He then stated that the manufacturer is in China and does not have US contact information.

Dicks is still selling this unit today but it is now called the 'Fitness Gear 2017 Pro Olympic Weightbench' .  The Web ID is 16FGEUFGPRLYMPCBNWGHA, the Style is: STE00403, and the SKU is 17403063.  The only different appears to be they changed some of the parts to blue instead of a dark grey.

Dicks feels that this is my problem and that I have to follow up with some manufacturer in China that has no presence in the USA.  I appealed to them that this is a serious safety concern and that something should be done.  Apparently Dicks no longer has the pictures I sent them, nor is interested in me resending to them.  From their response it appears nothing will be done.
justification: The weld failure poses a serious safety concern but no injury was reported.

incident_description:
I purchased a FitBit Charge 2 for Mother's Day, 2017. I received it a week later and started wearing it as instructed on the paperwork that came with it. It is supposed to be worn 24/7 since it tracks sleep patterns, heart rate, activity, etc. I have worn this tracker for the almost 2 months, This past Saturday, July 7th when I woke and took off the tracker to shower, I noticed a raised, red area on my right arm, It was itchy and was in the shape of the tracker with the two little dots for the charging ports. I showered, dried off and decided to wear the tracker on the left arm that day to give my right side a break, hoping that the marks would go away. Instead the next day the marks had darkened and by the third day my arm has a permanent raised burn that is shaped like the monitor. 

I clean this tracker everyday when I shower, I am a Nurses Aid and I wear this tracker instead of a watch, I sweat during the day, since my job is very physical. I also know a burn when I see one and my skin is permanently burned. The left arm that I wore the tracker on for one day has two slightly raised points, where the charging port came in contact with my skin. It is not as noticeable, however I can see them. There is definitely something wrong with this product. I went online after this happened and only then did I find out about this product and the fact that this company has had numerous complaints about its products, however continues to push them. I previously had a Fitbit One, which clips on to your clothing and is fully encased in a vinyl storage/case. I never had this problem with it. I moved over this the Charge 2 as gift to myself (an upgrade you may say) Well this gift really came back to bit me.
justification: The incident describes a permanent burn injury caused by the FitBit Charge 2, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The occurrence likelihood is set to 4 (likely) due to the user's report of similar complaints online.

incident_description: I have a Little Tikes green swing that has cracks in the upper and lower lips of the seat base where the ropes through it similar to the pink swing.  My green swing falls in the same model number and time frame as the pink swing.

incident_description:
2013 Kawasaki Mule 4010 MD ROV/UTV/ATV Rollover (1/4 passenger-side leaving).
12 year old female passenger (rear, right seat) suffered crushed outboard (right) lower leg during the rollover, which has required multiple surgeries, and is left with a horribly deformed leg.
Medical expenses are ~$300,000.

Kawasaki Mule is dangerously unstable.
Kawasaki Mule had no doors or nets to retain occupants in the vehicle during the rollover.
justification: The passenger suffered a severe injury requiring multiple surgeries, indicating a high severity level (3). The description suggests the vehicle's instability and lack of safety features make such incidents likely (4).

incident_description:
2012 Polaris Ranger RZR 170cc ROV/UTV/ATV rollover (3/4 driver-side leading roll).
13 year old male driver (belted and helmeted) instinctively grabbed the upright during the rollover, and sustained crush injuries to his outboard (left) hand.
All four (4) fingers of his left hand were traumatically and surgically amputated.
Driver is left with only a thumb and palm on his left hand.
Medical expenses exceed $260,000.
justification: The driver sustained severe crush injuries resulting in traumatic and surgical amputation of four fingers, which constitutes a significant injury.

incident_description:
I own a 2012 Ski Doo Tundra Sport.
The fuel tank has a design flaw.  The flaw involves a grommet that is immersed in fuel that is made of material that degrades when exposed to fuel.

I have a photograph of the deteriorated grommet ( that I am not able to attach here).

During the winter of 2017, a cataclysmic event was barely averted.  Several miles from home, while under way, I noticed that the fuel level was uncharacteristically dropping.  I smelled strong fuel vapors.  I shut off the unit and examined the engine compartment.  I observed fuel leaking from the tank.
It should be noted that had I applied the brakes before turning off the engine the uncontrolled fuel would have ignited, causing personal injury to myself and my passenger.

BRP has been notified.  The BRP representative has elected to dismiss my notification, and has refused to acknowledge the matter despite several communications.
justification: The incident involved a fuel leak that could have led to injury or death but was averted, resulting in no actual harm.

incident_description: A number of instructors and users have reported incidents of the seat and handlebars dropping suddenly during an indoor cycling class.  This is despite reminders at the beginning of classes to tighten the knobs which are supposed to hold the seat/handlebars in place.   Although most incidents have not resulted in severe injuries,  on at least two occasions, instructors fell due to the seat and handlebars suddenly dropping resulting in a torn quadricep (seat drop) and torn shoulder (handlebar drop).   Only about half of the 22 Keiser M3 cycles are usable due to the inability to tighten the seat or handlebar posts enough to prevent slippage.  A number of gym members refuse to use the Keiser M3 bikes.  The Keiser M3 bikes are only a few years old.  I am reporting this due to my belief that these bikes are dangerous for use by the consumer.  Keiser has changed the design and has the ability to retrofit the Keiser M3 cycles so that the seat and handlebar posts are not prone to slippage.  As with other indoor cycles, Keiser has added holes in the seat and handlebar posts and a peg to its friction system so when the tightening bolt loosens from the vibrations of use, the posts are locked in place.  A recall should be required to ensure public safety.
justification: The incident has resulted in injuries (torn quadricep and shoulder) and occurs frequently, with half of the bikes being unusable due to the issue.

incident_description: My son received his electric ripstick for Christmas in 2016. He has loved it and roughly 1 month ago, March 2017 he was riding his ripstick and the bolt holding the back wheel in place snapped and the wheel fell off while riding. No injuries occurred on this incident.

incident_description: We had purchased a zr1 Free Style Dirt Scooter for our son. He was riding it down a hill. Were he feel. His leg was caught on the scooter brake. incident_description: We had purchased a swimschool vest for our youngest daughter. Everything was fine until she went forward onto her stomach and she was trying to turn over but the vest kept her face down in the water. These vests need to be recalled before a child dies from it. Hospital told us exactly what vests to buy and they are the ones that are Coast Guard approved. They look like the vest you used on a boat.
justification: The child experienced a near-drowning incident requiring emergency medical attention, indicating an injury (severity 3). The occurrence likelihood is high (4) due to multiple similar incidents reported.

While using Model WESY86304 Weider Home Gym to do "Lat Pull Downs" in accordance with the Exercise Guide provided with the equipment the rear seat frame , part #16 , broke away from the bracket attaching it to the equipment. It appears the break occurred at the weld . 
I contacted ICON of Canada Inc. and they referred the matter to ICON Health and Fitness, Inc. 
in Logan Utah, 84321. 
I was fortunate to only suffer bruising with the sudden collapse of the seat as the sudden drop while exercising could easily have resulted in very serious and permanent injury. I conveyed the information to ICON Canada so that they  would be aware of the possible design flaw that could injure other users. Their approach was to send a "technician " who was not an engineer , metallurgist or welding expert to examine the equipment and conclude "the machine is in good condition and has no structural weakness". Yet the weld was broken and the seat  frame no longer attached to the bracket that mechanically attaches that seat to the equipment. 
ICON then began a process from the Canadian and USA offices to get me to sign a "waiver" and they would provide a replacement part of some type as the original part is no longer available . 
In researching the product , in my opinion , the seat design being a cantilever without support on the extremities is likely not strong enough for the designed purpose. All of ICON's current home gyms now have a seat frame that is supported at both ends. 
The Weider 8630 Home Gym , assembled and maintained as per instructions from the manufacturer has the potential to cause very serious injury to a user when the cantilevered seat /leg lift attachment is being used to perform exercises in accordance with the guide provided. In my attempt to prevent injury to others I was met with unsupportable statements from ICON on the design and manufacture of their product and in the end an over zealous attempt to get me to sign a release.
justification: The user suffered bruising from the equipment failure, which indicates an injury occurred. The incident could have resulted in more serious harm, suggesting a possible design flaw.

incident_description:
I own a Dahon Speed 7 folding bicycle. There are structural cracks in the frame. Please see attached photographs.

I, the sole rider of the bike, am well below the bicycle design maximums of 231 pounds weight and 6'3ÃÂ height (I am 170 lbs. and 5'8ÃÂ height.) The bike has been ridden solely on smooth roads, and has low mileage (I am estimating 2000-3000 miles based on tire usage.)

The frame has cracks at the top of the seat tube, already half-way around the tube on both sides, below the seatpost clamp. If the cracks continue, it will result in separation of the top portion of the tube, and seatpost, from the frame. The cracks also lead to the welds joining the top of the seat stays to the seat tube, possibly causing failure at that joint as well. Either of the above failures risk fall hazard and/or loss of bicycle control and risk of severe injury or death.

As reference, please see [REDACTED]; This [REDACTED] of a different bike brand involved ÃÂThe top clamp of the bicycle's seat post can crack, posing a fall hazard to the user.ÃÂ While due to a different part, this failure mode is similar to the failure mode above, and thus proves precedence with regard to it being a safety issue and the necessity of a recall if the failure proven. Please see link: https://www.cpsc.gov/[REDACTED]

This frame design is used on multiple Dahon bicycles. A quick search on the internet shows this failure mode to be common on this frame design.

I contend that the frame cracks are the result of a design defect. (I am a retired mechanical engineer and manager, and have authored patents of, among other things, clamped structural connections loaded in fatigue.) At the top of the seat tube is a slot parallel with the tube axis, to allow the seat post clamp to close the seat tube tightly around the seat post bushing and seat post. All bikes have a similar slot, but Dahon positioned the slot at the front of the tube, rather than the back of the tube as on all other bikes I have seen. The cracks initiate from the radius at the bottom of the slot, and propagate on each side circumferentially, progressing rapidly, as the crack increases the local stresses in a vicious cycle. When the rider sits on the bike, most of the force on the seat post is down, but due to the seat post angle, some is aft, which causes a bending moment (torque) into the seat tube, and this moment is especially high on Dahons due to the extremely long seat post, due to the folding design. That bending moment stresses the seat tube in tension in front, and compression in the back. This crack is a fatigue failure, and those only happen in tension, not compression. Thus, Dahon putting the clamping slot on the front of the seat tube introduced a weak point for a crack to initiate. Every other bike in the world puts this slot at the back of the seat tube, even other Dahons like the [REDACTED], which would put the slot in compression. Placing the slot on the front of the tube is a design defect. However, having the slot on the back, while definitely improving durability, would not guarantee no failure, if the stress in front still exceeded the fatigue life limits of the material. The seat tube is highly stressed; ****Notably, later models of this same bike are equipped with an aluminum bushing at this interface between the seat post and the seat tube, I believe to strengthen this area. The failed frame in question is equipped with the earlier plastic bushing, which is lower strength and less rigid.****

I communicated the frame failure, with detailed description as noted above, and photographs, to the local Dahon dealer, who forwarded them to the manufacturer, Dahon USA. The manufacturer has refused to replace or repair the frame, saying the failure is due to excessive seat post extension (my seat post is 1.5ÃÂ below maximum extension, it would be impossible for me to ride with the seatpost higher because I am 5'8ÃÂ), and the bike is out of warranty, despite this being a ****safety issue****.


What I am requesting from CPSC:
Ask Dahon:
What was the reason for the change from plastic to aluminum for the seat post bushing, and,
Has Dahon completed cyclic fatigue testing, at maximum design rider weight (231 lbs.) and maximum design seatpost extension (equal to 6'3ÃÂ rider height, maximum mark on the seat post), to confirm if this is a valid solution to the seat tube failures on this frame design.

If the aluminum seat post bushing is ****proven**** to prevent frame failures, I would require the manufacturer, Dahon USA, to:
Replace any frames with cracks at the upper seatpost, and,
Replace the plastic seatpost bushing with the newer aluminum seat post bushing, including on frames with no cracks, as a preventive measure.

If, however, the aluminum seatpost bushing is ****not proven**** to prevent the frame failure as noted, I would request that CPSC require Dahon to:
- Replace completely, all frames of this design, with frames proven to not fail in this manner.

Best regards,

[REDACTED]
Mechanical Engineering Manager (retired)


Attachments: photographs of failure











filename: Dahon frame crack CPSC letter
justification: The frame cracks pose a risk of severe injury or death if they lead to structural failure while riding, and the issue is described as common for this frame design.

incident_description: My daughter has a Pacific Cycle model R1493TR Mongoose bicycle which has hand brakes only - no coaster brake.  The brakes are insufficient to stop the bike from any reasonable riding speed and do not meet the requirements of the federal regulation which is to stop in 15 feet from 15 mph.  I rode the bike myself and was able to continue to ride with minimal additional effort with the brakes fully applied. incident_description: Our family purchased a 2016 Polaris turbo RZR for us to enjoy off road adventures together. Polaris advertised the 2016 RZR as "the worlds most complete high performance side by side. Extreme performance for 4, with no trade offs or compromises. The extended wheel base and exclusive FOX internal bypass shocks work with the industries most advanced side by side suspension to tame the gnarliest terrain you can find". Since our purchase we've been patient with the numerous recalls which have made my wife and I question the Polaris product line. We have an annual family trip to Sand Mountain NV every year to enjoy the dunes, explore the pony express trail as well as numerous ghost towns. This year while riding the dunes in our Polaris RZR we had a suspension component fail. It was a right rear lower radius rod. Ground conditions were steep and sandy. All four of us, myself [REDACTED], my wife [REDACTED] and our kids age 10 and 12 were all in the RZR for a ride. We had rode on and off most of the day, jumping small dunes and riding up and down the large drag hill (comp hill). As the afternoon came to an end we were, what's referred to as "rain bowing" on the slope of a tall dune. Rain bowing is when a person operates a vehicle up a slope turning in an arc at the top while they still have momentum and drives back down. The path is in the shape of a rainbow when a person looks at the tracks. We had done this maneuver several times driving through the tracks from previous passes at an average speed of 30 m.p.h. The last time we went up I turned our arc to the right at the top of the dune the RZR bouncing up and down through our old tracks as it had done many times prior. However this time I felt the right rear of the vehicle fall below normal ride height as well as a strong drag that slowed the vehicle. As it slowed and leaned more to the right, I knew we were going over. My attempt to steer the front end down the hill was to no avail, the RZR with my entire family in it, rolled all the way over. As the RZR rolled back to the wheels I turned to the right (down hill) and floored the accelerator in hopes to stop the vehicle from rolling more. It moved the front end down the hill but not enough, we rolled over again, and again when the vehicle landed on the wheels I turned right and accelerated. I continued this till the front end of the RZR moved down the hill enough to stop the machine from rolling. It was 5-1/4 rolls before we stopped, on its side, about 1/3 of the way down the hill and I immediately shut the engine off. We asked the kids if they were ok. All of us were stunned, bruised and completely covered with sand. As other riders quickly arrived on site I placed the RZR in park and myself and two other men lifted the RZR back to its wheels. The outer body was wrecked; the roof, doors and two of the wheel I had received for Christmas were destroyed. We contacted Polaris and since we bought a 5-year warranty with this vehicle the service manager has us bring it in to open a warranty claim. Since then Polaris moved it to a safety claim and submitted it to their engineering department. We've also been researching the part failure on the internet and have found a lot of other Polaris RZR customers have had the same issue with broken radius rods. While at the dealership and also during my internet research we've learned that Polaris has upgraded the part that is breaking on the 2017 models.
justification: The incident resulted in bruises and the family being stunned, indicating minor injuries, hence severity level 3. The occurrence likelihood is 4 (likely) due to multiple reports of similar part failures.

incident_description:
My daughter was exercising on a Johnson Health Tech "Matrix Fitness" Elliptical exercise machine (http://www.matrixfitness.com/en/cardio/ellipticals) when her foot slipped forward off the foot pad and then was pinched between the foot pad and the body of the machine. This violently twisted her ankle and possibly tore tendons and caused a metacarpal fracture. 

The design of this machine is dangerous due to a combination of three specific design flaws:

1. The design of the foot pad does not effectively prevent the foot from slipping forward. There is only a low (less than 1" high) rim at the forward edge of the foot pad.

2. There is not enough clearance between the forward edge of the foot pad in its most forward position and the body of the machine. The clearance of approximately 1" is not enough to accommodate a foot that has slipped off the foot pad due to the previous design flaw.

3. Even at low speed, the momentum of the machine pushes the foot pad forward with sufficient force to cause serious injury to a foot that has slipped off the foot pad and has been caught in the pinch point between the foot pad and the body of the machine.
justification: The incident resulted in a twisted ankle, possible tendon tear, and metacarpal fracture, indicating a severity level of 3 (Injury). The occurrence likelihood is 4 (likely) due to the described design flaws that could lead to similar injuries.

incident_description:
I was riding my ~5-7 year old mountain bike yesterday when the Axle (RockShox Maxle, SRAM) failed and caused me to fall. The crash resulted in a deep laceration and high-speed impact of my patella on a rock. I did not seek emergency care because I do not have any apparent knee joint injury. I do, however, have swelling that limits ambulation and required me to take a day off of Medical school. 

The failure was at a location not in contact with the frame or any other component, but at the beginning of the threading on the axle (this is an obvious product flaw), and there are numerous reports of this product breaking on message boards online, with no recall. I was riding over small rocks on a large-travel suspension bicycle (light normal conditions) and there was no evident impact or strike at the time it broke. Furthermore, the wheel is perfectly true, derailleur hanger (immediately next to the break point and designed to break) is intact, and there is literally no other damage to the bike except the shearing of 4 spoke nipples, presumably from the excessive torque after the axle broke. This is a large-diameter axle designed for aggressive downhill use, and it should never be the failure point on a bicycle. I truly was not interested in suing, but when I contacted SRAM for a replacement, I was told that it is outside of the 2-year warranty and they only communicate with dealers. There is a systemic issue of neglect with this company that is obviously evident in their communications, and I believe somebody will get seriously inured if it persists.
justification: The incident resulted in a deep laceration and significant swelling requiring time off, indicating an injury (severity 3). The product has a history of similar failures, making recurrence likely (likelihood 4).
